newsitem.title: USA: Experts disagree over employee motivation plans.
newsitem.headline: Experts disagree over employee motivation plans.

text.p: The kind of incentives a company uses to motivate its employees may matter less than the fact it is making a genuine effort.

Consider the popular "Employee-of-the-Month" photos hoteliers hang in their lobbies. Bob Losyk, president of Innovative Training Solutions, in Ft. Lauderdale, Fla., says they work "extremely well," particularly if tied to "a criteria of quality goals or service behaviours."
Businesses "want their customers to see that they value their customers and their employees," Losyk writes in his new book "Managing A Changing Workforce" (Workplace Trends).
But Jerry McAdams, a reward systems expert with human resources firm Watson Wyatt Worldwide, in St. Louis, says they create more "losers" than "winners."

"Does it make sense that there really will be an outstanding performer every time?" asks McAdams in his book, "The Reward Plan Advantage" (Jossey-Bass). "Those 'Walls of Fame' thrive only because they are the easiest," he says.

"I'm amazed at the way people don't understand the difference between recognition and performance improvement efforts," McAdams said. "Recognition is after the fact. The mistake most companies make is that they think their recognition plans are doing the job of performance improvement efforts and they can't. The reality is that they need both."
So do the incentives work or not?

At Marriott Corp., "Each hotel decides on its own" whether to use Wall of Fame promotions, said Vicki McCracken, Marriott's regional human resources director. "I see them in some hotels and not in others. Their effectiveness depends on how you use them."

Which suggests there's no "right" or "wrong" in incentive design. What is certain, McAdams said, is that managers who once thought of employees as "a cost of doing business" now think of them "as assets."
Regrettably, he added, companies are still "wary" of spending the "significant sums on employee performance improvement" that they lavish on quality or cycle time reduction.
Employers, though, do spend to motivate employees. "Incentive" magazine put last year's bill at $19.5 billion.
Seven of 10 "Fortune 1000" executives told St. Louis-based Maritz Performance Improvement Co. that they use incentive plans.
In addition, 91 percent of executives surveyed by Towers Perrin give "favorable ratings" to their own reward plans, indicating they do believe they work.

"Cash- or stock-based reward programmes," the survey concluded, "go further in building employee acceptance, sustaining interest, and, most important, achieving quantifiable performance improvements."

Automaker Honda is one company that spends. It pays "associates" at its Marysville, Ohio, operations $2 million a year for their suggestions -- and reaps $6 million in cost savings, spokesperson Sharon Van Winkle said.
"Associates" earn anywhere from $50 to a new car and global airline tickets, plus extra vacation and base pay.

Cash counts, Maritz says, but the better plans mix in feedback, communications, and training. Firms that give travel or merchandise, give "symbols of success participants can proudly 'show off' to their family and friends," Maritz adds.
Jerry Galuten, president of New York's SGD International Corp., a leading barter firm, showers his staff with treats such as breakfast in Cancun, lunch in Jamaica or day trips to Aruba.
Sentinel Systems, an "Inc. 500" security company in Hampton, Va., rewards star employees with a week-long Caribbean luxury cruise.

Some 120 firms reward their workers with Maritz's new debit MasterCard, issued by The Boatmen's National Bank, in St. Louis. Award pay is deposited directly into workers' accounts, good for purchases at 35,000 outlets.
According to Maritz's own survey of cardholders, 65 percent of them say the card motivates them to work harder.

"Incentive plans such as Honda's and Boatman's," McAdams said, "reward performance in a proactive way as opposed to a reactive way. Such plans are powerful but underused. They can make a huge difference in a company's competitive environment."
(Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
